summary: Describes how IPv6 is supported in 3GPP's Evolved Packet System, the cellular architecture behind HSPA and LTE. Operators face a shortage of IPv4 addresses and increasing pressure to move to IPv6. It is informational guidance for the mobile world.

plainLanguage.summary: Phones use up internet addresses, and the old kind is running out. This explains how mobile networks can give phones the newer, roomier IPv6 addresses.

questions: how do mobile operators deploy ipv6
how do phones get ipv6 addresses
what is ipv4v6 dual stack bearer
subtitle: How IPv6 works in 3GPP mobile networks, from PDP contexts and bearers to address setup and dual-stack deployment.

tldr.problem: Operators running 3GPP cellular networks face IPv4 address shortages and pressure to move to IPv6, but need to know how IPv6 fits the architecture.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how a phone gets a connection to a gateway (PDP context or PDN connection), how it receives a /64 prefix by stateless autoconfiguration, and how dual-stack IPv4v6 bearers work from Release-8.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational overview. Dual-stack keeps IPv4 fallback but does not reduce the IPv4 addresses used, and IPv6-only access needs testing of applications first.

today: RFC 6459 is an Informational document and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the state of 3GPP IPv6 support as of January 2012.

sections.title: IPv6 in Cellular Networks
sections.content:
IPv6 has been part of the 3GPP standards since the first release (Release 99). Even so, the RFC says commercial IPv6 deployment remains low, mainly for lack of business incentive, as in other networks.

The newest architecture is the Evolved Packet System (EPS), also called SAE, LTE or Release-8, which is packet-centric. With subscribers growing and IANA's IPv4 space depleted, operators and vendors are working out how to deploy IPv6. The RFC gives an overview of how IPv6 is supported by the current 3GPP specifications and discusses deployment issues. It lists two goals for transition: IPv4-only devices keep working, and dual-stack devices can use IPv6 or IPv4 depending on the application, the bearers and the servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile networks have supported the newer address style for a long time, but few have switched on. This document shows how it works and why switching is tricky.

sections.title: Gateways, APNs and Bearers
sections.content:
A phone (the UE) reaches the Internet through a gateway: the GGSN in 2G/3G GPRS, or the PDN-GW in EPS. Gateways are found by an Access Point Name (APN), which is a domain name that uses the DNS. A UE can be attached to several gateways at once, for example one for the Internet and one for operator services.

In GPRS the link to a gateway is a PDP context. In EPS it is a PDN connection. Each is tied to one IPv4 address and/or one /64 IPv6 prefix, and looks like a network interface on the UE. EPS PDN types are IPv4, IPv6 and IPv4v6 from Release-8. GPRS gained the IPv4v6 type in Release-9.

An EPS bearer carries IP flows that need the same forwarding treatment. A default bearer is set up at start-up, so the UE gets an address right away, unlike GPRS. Dedicated bearers carry flows needing special treatment and share the default bearer's address. Guaranteed Bit Rate (GBR) bearers have resources reserved, while the default bearer is always non-GBR.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone connects to the internet through a gateway door with a name. Each connection is like a separate pipe, and it gets its own address.

sections.title: Address Configuration
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are given during PDP context or bearer setup. DHCPv4 is supported but not widely used, so the UE must always support setup through the bearer signaling.

For IPv6, Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 4862) is the only supported method. Stateful DHCPv6 is not supported by 3GPP, but stateless DHCPv6 for other settings is. So the M-bit is always zero in the Router Advertisement, and the O-bit may be one.

  • Each default bearer gets a unique /64 prefix. The network suggests an Interface Identifier at layer 2, and the UE must use it for its link-local address.
  • The L-bit in the Prefix Information Option must be zero, so the prefix is not used for on-link determination. If the prefix is used for SLAAC, the A-bit must be one.
  • Only one /64 prefix per bearer is possible. A UE that sees more than one prefix considers only the first. Multihoming within a bearer and renumbering without closing the layer-2 connection are not possible.
  • Because the gateway guarantees the prefix is unique, the UE does not need Duplicate Address Detection for its addresses.

Prefix delegation comes with Release-10 and uses DHCPv6 prefix delegation (RFC 3633). Before that, the UE can share its /64 to a local network with an ND proxy (RFC 4389).
sections.plainLanguage: The network hands each phone its own street of addresses. The phone builds its own house number on that street, and because the street is only its own, it does not have to check for clashes.

sections.title: Dual-Stack Connections and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
Before Release-8, a dual-stack phone opened two parallel PDP contexts, one IPv4 and one IPv6. The RFC calls this not optimal, because it doubles signaling and uses more network resources. From Release-8 a single IPv4v6 PDN connection or bearer carries both. From Release-9 GPRS nodes also support IPv4v6 PDP contexts.

Setting up a PDN connection involves the UE attach request, authentication with the HSS/AAA, a Create Session request passed from the MME through the SGW to the PDN-GW (where the address or prefix is assigned), and then radio bearer setup. After the Attach Complete the UE can send uplink data, and downlink data including SLAAC packets follows. If the UE names no type, a dual-stack connection is the default in Release-8 networks.

The 3GPP link resembles a point-to-point link without link-layer addresses. The RFC lists problems when a UE stack treats it as IEEE 802: Neighbor Advertisements may lack a Target Link-Layer Address option, or a GGSN may drop Neighbor Solicitations, so address resolution never finishes and IPv6 traffic stalls. Some operating systems also discard Router Advertisements on PPP links, which makes SLAAC fail.
sections.plainLanguage: It used to take two pipes to use both address types. Now one pipe does both. Some phones also get confused by the pipe and wait forever for an answer.

sections.title: Deployment Issues
sections.content:
Dual-stack gives an IPv4 fallback and keeps legacy devices working, but it does not lower the number of IPv4 addresses used, because every dual-stack bearer still needs an IPv4 address, private or public. Operators often use private RFC 1918 addresses. About 16 million UEs can get a unique private address, which many operators exceed, so they reuse ranges across gateways or areas and use NAT44.

Mobility has limits. If a UE may hand over between a Release-8 LTE network and a pre-Release-9 2G/3G network without an S4-SGSN, only single-stack bearers are used. Inter-RAT handovers need IPv4v6, IPv6 and IPv4 bearers to map one to one, so provisioning follows the lowest common denominator.

An IPv6-only bearer works in 3GPP, but reaching the IPv4 Internet needs translation such as NAT64 (RFC 6144), which the Release-8 architecture does not describe. Inter-operator roaming networks were all IPv4 only at the time, and 3GPP gives no standard way to block IPv6 roaming without also disabling IPv4. Release-8 UEs request IPv4v6 if dual-stack and may fall back based on cause codes #50, #51 and #52.
sections.plainLanguage: Using both address types keeps old phones working, but you still need the old addresses too. Roaming and handing over between old and new towers make switching harder.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that it introduces no security-related concerns. The UE and network authenticate each other during attach. Each new connection or address assignment can be authorized against the PCC infrastructure or the PDN's AAA server. The control plane is always at least integrity and replay protected.

The point-to-point link, with only the UE and the first-hop router on it, mitigates several on-link and Neighbor Discovery attacks. Off-link IPv6 attacks affect EPS as much as any IPv6 system. Using an IMSI as the Interface Identifier would allow tracking, so it is prohibited, though no standard method blocks misbehaving UEs.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone and network check each other's identity. Because only two devices share each pipe, many tricks do not work, but a phone must not build its address from its secret ID number.
